did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ecclesiastes presents wealth and honor not as guaranteed blessings, but as part of a reality that can become an “evil” if a person does not enjoy what he has been given.

Did you know? The chapter describes a man who has wealth, possessions, and honor, lacking nothing he desires—yet he is not allowed to enjoy the fruits of his riches, and a stranger consumes them instead.

Did you know? Even a man who has a hundred children and lives for many years is not considered happy by Ecclesiastes if his soul is not satisfied with good things; he is not even given an honorable burial.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes compares such a person’s condition to that of a stillborn child: both are described as coming in futility and departing in darkness, but the stillborn child does not experience the hardships and disappointments of life.
Did you know? Even an exceptionally long life—even two thousand years—does not guarantee goodness or satisfaction; in the end, everyone goes to the same place.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes a person’s labor as effort directed toward his mouth—that is, toward satisfying his needs—but adds that the soul is never completely filled.

Did you know? The chapter asks what advantage the wise have over fools, and what the poor person gains by knowing how to conduct himself among the living; these questions highlight the limits of human advantage and the difficulty of finding certainty.
Did you know? The expression “Better what the eyes see than the wandering of desire” favors what is present and visible over the restless pursuit of things that have not yet been attained.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes reminds people that they have already been given a name and are known as human beings, and therefore cannot argue or contend with one who is stronger than they are—a statement of human powerlessness before reality.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Ecclesiastes emphasizes that a person does not know with certainty what is good for him during his fleeting days, which pass like a shadow, nor what will happen after him under the sun.
